sentences.text: Adasaurus was a large dromaeosaurid that grew to between 2.39 and 3.5 meters in length, with a body mass ranging from 36.4 to 87 kilograms.
Unlike its relatives, this animal had a sickle claw that was small and blunt, showing signs of reduced use, along with a uniquely curved lacrimal bone.
The lacrimal bone formed an inverted L-shape with a thin, curved body, a specific trait also observed in the genus Austroraptor.
In the holotype specimen, the scapula and coracoid bones were completely fused into a single scapulocoracoid structure with no visible suture line between them.
Measurements of the leg bones show the femur reached 27.3 centimeters in length while the tibia measured 30.3 centimeters.
The animal was first illustrated by Rinchen Barsbold in 1977 but remained an informally named taxon until it received a formal description.
Rinchen Barsbold formally named Adasaurus and its type species A. mongoliensis in 1983 based on two partial specimens.
The name combines the Mongolian word for evil spirit with the Greek word for lizard.
The holotype and paratype specimens were unearthed from the Bügiin Tsav locality in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
Researchers in 2006 suggested that Adasaurus used its sickle claw less frequently than other deinonychosaurs due to the lack of asymmetrical ridges on its lower heel.
In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues proposed the 'Raptor Prey Restraint' model, suggesting dromaeosaurids pinned prey with their body weight and sickle claws before feeding.
Peter Bishop could not confirm or deny whether the sickle claw function was lost or retained in Adasaurus, noting its unusually small size and unique ginglymoid structure.
Adasaurus is a member of Dromaeosauridae, a group closely related to living birds.
Revisions indicate that Adasaurus belongs to the Velociraptorinae subfamily, which includes lightly built animals like Velociraptor.
While traditionally assigned to Dromaeosaurinae, several analyses suggest Adasaurus belongs to Velociraptorinae.
Adasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 68 million years ago, in the Nemegt Formation.
The environment of Adasaurus included stream channels, mudflats, and shallow lakes within the Nemegt Formation.
In 2010, Phil Senter disputed the authenticity of the reduced sickle claw in Adasaurus, claiming the bone did not belong to the specimen.
